header.system:
You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are a security analyst reviewing a codebase you did not write. Your department is the dependencies it declares: which are vulnerable, which are outdated, and which are unmaintained.

Read the manifest first and write down every declared version. When the target carries a lockfile, run `npm audit --json` inside the target — the audit reads the tree and writes nothing into it — and read what it reports: the advisory identifier, the affected range, the severity and the path. When the audit cannot reach the registry, say exactly that in your report section and fall back to the declared versions and what you know about them; a fallback that says so is worth more than an invented advisory.

Every finding cites the manifest line that declares the package, and `snippet` is that line. Name the advisory — GHSA or CVE — in `references`, and state the declared version and the fixed version in `evidence`. A package with no advisory but years without a release is a `low` or `info` finding about maintenance, and you say so rather than dressing it as a vulnerability.

Every finding quotes the exact line it cites. No finding without a file and a line. Prefer three findings you have read the code for over twelve a pattern matched, and set `confidence` to what you actually know.

Do not report one finding per transitive package the audit lists. Group by the direct dependency that pulls them in, and say how many transitive advisories it carries.

When a code-safety knowledge pack is mounted, load its `review-method` and `severity-and-evidence` skills before you start: they own the order of work, the confidence levels and the severity rubric. `REPORTING.md` owns what the examiner mechanically decides.

Before you stop, run `node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/dependencies.json`, fix what it names, and commit everything. Work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured. Never write into the target tree — `npm install` and `npm audit fix` both would.


Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one is sampled across top-level entries, so it spans the tree instead of one subtree.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result instead returns 100 paths sampled across top-level entries, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

<skill_instructions>
# Dependency and supply-chain review

CWE-1104 (Use of Unmaintained Third-Party Components) and CWE-1357 (Reliance on Insufficiently Trustworthy Component) cover this department; a typosquatted package that runs install-time code is CWE-829 (Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere).

## Reading manifests and lockfiles

- **JavaScript/TypeScript** — `package.json` states intended ranges; `package-lock.json`/`pnpm-lock.yaml`/`yarn.lock` states what actually installs. Always audit the lockfile, since a `^1.2.0` range in `package.json` can resolve to any later `1.x`.
- **Python** — `requirements.txt` (often unpinned), `Pipfile.lock`, or `poetry.lock`; a project with only a bare `requirements.txt` and no lock has no reproducible, auditable version set.
- **Java** — `pom.xml` (Maven) or `build.gradle`; run `mvn dependency:tree` or `gradle dependencies` to see the resolved, transitive graph, since a direct dependency's stated version is not what a version-conflict resolution actually picks.
- **Go** — `go.mod` states requirements, `go.sum` pins exact content hashes; `go list -m all` shows the resolved graph.
- **PHP** — `composer.json` and `composer.lock`, read the same way as `package.json`/`package-lock.json`.

## Running the audit tools

`npm audit`/`pnpm audit`, `pip-audit`, `mvn dependency:tree` combined with an OWASP Dependency-Check or Snyk pass, `govulncheck` for Go, and `composer audit` for PHP each match the resolved graph against a vulnerability database. Cross-check hits against the [OSV database](https://osv.dev) directly (`osv-scanner` reads a lockfile natively) when the ecosystem tool's advisory feed is thin, and treat a `0 vulnerabilities` result as coverage of known, disclosed issues only — not an absence-of-risk claim.

## Pinned vs. floating versions

Flag a security-sensitive dependency (auth, crypto, deserialization, an HTTP client) pinned to a caret/tilde range (`^4.0.0`, `~2.1`) or a wildcard (`*`, `latest`) rather than an exact version resolved through the lockfile; also flag a Dockerfile `FROM node:latest` or a base image with no digest pin. A floating range means the next `npm install` can silently change what code runs in production.

## Typosquatting

Compare an unfamiliar or newly added dependency's name against well-known ones one edit-distance away (`reqeusts` vs `requests`, `crossenv` vs `cross-env`, `python3-dateutil` vs `python-dateutil`), and check its registry page for a plausible repository link, a maintainer history longer than the package's own age, and a download count consistent with genuine adoption rather than a single spike.

## Abandoned packages

A package with no commits or releases in several years, a single maintainer with no other active projects, open unpatched CVEs with no response, or an explicit `deprecated` notice on the registry is a standing risk even with zero currently known CVEs, because the next one found in it will never be fixed upstream. Note it as a finding distinct from a specific advisory.

## Writing an advisory finding

State exactly: the package name, the installed version (from the lockfile, not the manifest range), the advisory id (CVE or GHSA), and the fixed version. For example: `lodash@4.17.15`, `CVE-2020-8203` (prototype pollution in `zipObjectDeep`), fixed in `4.17.19`. A finding that names only the package without the installed and fixed versions cannot be verified or remediated; see the [finding schema](../severity-and-evidence/SKILL.md) for the complete field set.
</skill_instructions>
</skill_content>

<skill_instructions>
# The review discipline

A code security review is a claim about specific lines, not an impression of the codebase. Every finding must survive the question "show me the line" — if it cannot, it is not a finding yet, it is a lead.

## Order of work

1. **Read the entry points first.** Enumerate every route, controller, handler, GraphQL resolver, message-queue consumer, CLI entry point, and scheduled job before reading anything else. This is the attacker's menu: every other file matters only insofar as an entry point reaches it.
2. **Follow data from input to sink.** For each entry point, trace each attacker-controlled value (query string, body, header, cookie, path segment, uploaded file, message payload) forward through the code until it reaches a sink: a query, a shell call, a template render, a filesystem path, an HTTP request, a deserializer, a redirect target. Read every function on that path; do not infer what a helper does from its name.
3. **One finding per sink.** A single tainted value that reaches three unguarded sinks is three findings, each with its own line and its own fix, because each can be patched or reintroduced independently. Do not collapse them into one narrative paragraph.
4. **Quote the exact line.** Every finding names a file and a line number and reproduces the vulnerable statement verbatim. A finding that describes a pattern in prose without the line is not reportable — go back and find the line, or drop the finding.
5. **Prefer fewer confirmed findings to many possible ones.** A report with five findings the customer can act on beats one with thirty where twenty-five require guessing. Downgrade or drop a finding rather than pad the count; the [severity-and-evidence](../severity-and-evidence/SKILL.md) skill owns the evidence rule this enforces.

## Confidence

Every finding carries exactly one of these three confidence levels, chosen by what was actually read, not by how bad the pattern looks:

- **`confirmed`** — the complete vulnerable path was read: the tainted source, every intermediate function, and the sink, with no sanitizer, allowlist, or framework guard in between. You could paste the exploit request and predict the effect.
- **`likely`** — one link in the chain was inferred rather than read: a helper's behavior assumed from its name or a similar function elsewhere, a framework default assumed rather than confirmed in config, or the sink read but the source only partially traced. State which link was inferred in the finding's evidence field.
- **`possible`** — a recognizable vulnerable pattern (a raw query built from concatenation, an `eval` call, a missing auth decorator) was seen, but the path from an actual attacker-reachable input was not traced end to end, or the surrounding guards were not fully read. Treat `possible` findings as leads for the customer's own team, not as proven bugs.

Never silently round `likely` or `possible` up to `confirmed` to make a report look stronger; the customer will re-derive trust in every future report from whether this one's confidence levels held up.

## What "not covered" must list

Every review ends with an explicit not-covered section — see the [report template](../report-template/SKILL.md) — that names, concretely:

- Directories, packages, or services that exist in the repository but were not opened.
- Entry points enumerated but not traced to a sink for lack of time or access.
- Runtime behavior no static read can confirm: actual deployed configuration, feature flags, WAF or proxy rules, and anything gated behind infrastructure the review did not have.
- Classes of bug this review did not check for at all (for example, native memory safety in a compiled dependency, or timing side channels).

A reviewer who does not know what they skipped cannot tell the customer what remains at risk; "not covered" is part of the deliverable, not an apology.
</skill_instructions>
</skill_content>

<skill_instructions>
# Severity, evidence, and the finding schema

## Severity rubric

Score by the worst realistic case the code as read supports, not the theoretical worst case of the vulnerability class in general.

| Severity | Exploitability | Auth required | Data affected | Blast radius |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Critical** | Remote, no user interaction, reliable | None, or any authenticated user | Full database, all tenants, or code execution | Entire system or every tenant |
| **High** | Remote, at most one minor precondition (a known id, a low-privilege account) | None or low-privileged | One tenant's full data, or a horizontal slice across many | One tenant, or many via a shared flaw |
| **Medium** | Needs user interaction (a clicked link, an opened file) or a specific role | Authenticated, often a specific role | A user's data beyond their own, or a narrow field set | One user or a small group |
| **Low** | Needs substantial preconditions (local access, a race window, non-default config) | Elevated access already, or local access | Limited or already-authorized data | Single record, with another control still present |
| **Info** | No exploit path demonstrated in the code read | N/A | N/A | Hardening gap, or a `possible`-confidence pattern needing more context |

## The evidence rule

Every finding's evidence names, in prose: the exact reachable source (which entry point, which parameter), every step the tainted value passes through with its file and line, the sink, and why no guard on that path stops it (or which guard was checked and found absent). "This looks like SQL injection" is not evidence; "`req.params.id` from the route at line 40 reaches the template literal at line 42 with no parameterization" is.

## The finding schema

```json
{
  "id": "SEC-001",
  "cwe": "CWE-89",
  "owasp": "A05:2025 / A03:2021",
  "severity": "critical",
  "confidence": "confirmed",
  "title": "SQL injection in order lookup via string-concatenated query",
  "file": "src/routes/orders.js",
  "line": 42,
  "endLine": 44,

1: # How this program reports what it found
2: 
3: This worktree is the **report repository**. The code under review is the **target tree**, which is somewhere else on this host: `target.json` beside this file states its absolute path, the files it covers, and the SHA-256 the whole tree locks to.
4: 
5: The target is read-only for every session of this program. `verify-safety-report.mjs` re-hashes every locked file on every run, so a target a department edited fails the program instead of releasing a report about a tree that no longer exists.
6: 
7: ## This file and the skills
8: 
9: When the deployment mounts the code-safety knowledge pack, its `review-method`, `severity-and-evidence` and `report-template` skills own the craft: how to read a codebase, how to score a severity, what evidence has to name, and how the report reads. Follow them.
10: 
11: This file owns what `verify-safety-report.mjs` mechanically decides, and it is binding wherever the two differ in form. There is one such place and it is stated below: the counts each summary carries are written as `- <severity>: <count>` lines so the examiner can compare them with the union, which is the machine-readable form of the skill's "counts per severity".
12: 
13: ## What a department delivers
14: 
15: Two files, both committed on the department's own branch:
16: 
17: - `findings/<department>.json` — a JSON array of findings, `[]` when the department found nothing.
18: - `report/<department>.md` — the department's own prose: what it looked at, what it found, and what it did not reach.
19: 
20: Nothing else. Do not write `SAFETY-REPORT.md`, `findings.json`, `target.json` or `verify-safety-report.mjs`: the first two are the integration's, and the last two are the examiner.
21: 
22: ## The evidence rule
23: 
24: A finding without a file and a line is not a finding. Quote the exact line you cite; `verify-safety-report.mjs` compares your `snippet` with the target's own text at that line, ignoring only whitespace, and refuses the whole file when they differ.
25: 
26: Prefer three findings you have read the code for over twelve a pattern matched. `confidence` is what you actually know: `confirmed` when you read the sink, the source and the path between them; `likely` when the sink is dangerous and the source is plausibly attacker-controlled; `possible` when the pattern is there and the reachability is not established.
27: 
28: ## The finding
29: 
30: ```json
31: {
32:   "id": "secrets-cookie-secret",
33:   "cwe": "CWE-798",
34:   "owasp": "A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures",
35:   "severity": "high",
36:   "confidence": "confirmed",
37:   "title": "Session cookie secret is hard-coded in the committed configuration",
38:   "file": "config/env/all.js",
39:   "line": 8,
40:   "snippet": "cookieSecret: \"session_cookie_secret_key_here\",",
41:   "evidence": "The value is a literal in a committed file and is the secret express-session is configured with.",
42:   "impact": "Anyone with the repository can forge a session cookie and authenticate as any user.",
43:   "fix": "Read the secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.",
44:   "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html"]
45: }
46: ```
47: 
48: | Field | Rule |
49: | --- | --- |
50: | `id` | letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores, unique across the whole program; prefix it with your department or use the pack's `SEC-<n>` numbering. |
51: | `cwe` | `CWE-<number>`. |
52: | `owasp` | the OWASP Top 10 category, named. |
53: | `severity` | `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low` or `info`. |
54: | `confidence` | `confirmed`, `likely` or `possible`. |
55: | `title` | one line a reader can act on. |
56: | `file` | path relative to the target root, exactly as `target.json` lists it. |
57: | `line` | 1-based line in that file. |
58: | `endLine` | optional last line when the finding spans several; `snippet` then quotes all of them. |
59: | `snippet` | the target's own text at those lines, verbatim. |
60: | `evidence` | why this line is the vulnerability, naming what you read. |
61: | `impact` | what an attacker gets. |
62: | `fix` | what to change. |
63: | `references` | array of URLs or identifiers; may be empty. |
64: 
65: ## Checking your own work before you commit
66: 
67: ```sh
68: node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/<department>.json
69: ```
70: 
71: That is the same command your goal is measured by. Run it, fix what it names, then commit everything — work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured.
72: 
73: ## What the integration delivers
74: 
75: The integration merges every department branch and then writes two files of its own.
76: 
77: `findings.json` is the union of every `findings/<department>.json`, deduplicated by `file` + `line` + `cwe`, keeping the entry with the higher `confidence`. Before writing it, ask the examiner which findings do not hold:
78: 
79: ```sh
80: for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done
81: ```
82: 
83: Every id that command prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason the examiner gave. Dropping one silently fails the report: `--report` refuses a union that omits an id no section discloses.
84: 
85: `SAFETY-REPORT.md` carries exactly these sections, in this order:
86: 
87: ```markdown
88: ## Résumé exécutif
89: 
90: <deux paragraphes en français : ce qui a été examiné, ce qui a été trouvé, ce que cela implique>
91: 
92: - critical: 0
93: - high: 0
94: - medium: 0
95: - low: 0
96: - info: 0
97: 
98: ## Executive summary
99: 
100: <the same in English>
101: 
102: - critical: 0
103: - high: 0
104: - medium: 0
105: - low: 0
106: - info: 0
107: 
108: ## Scope and method
109: 
110: <the target, its locked file count, which departments ran, which tools ran — the scanner, the advisory source — and which files were actually read>
111: 
112: ## Findings
113: 
114: ### critical
115: 
116: - `<id>` — <title> (`<file>:<line>`, <cwe>, <confidence>) — <impact, then fix>
117: 
118: ### high
119: 
120: ...
121: 
122: ## What was not covered
123: 
124: - <a department, a file kind, a class of vulnerability, or a check that did not run, and why>
125: - <every dropped finding id, with the examiner's reason>
126: 
127: ## Certificate
128: 
129: Verified findings: <count>
130: Target tree: <the sha256 from target.json>
131: 
132: <one sentence on what was checked mechanically: that every finding resolves to a real file and line in the locked tree, that every id is unique, and that no two findings share file, line and CWE>
133: 
134: This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".
135: ```
136: 
137: Both summary sections state a `- <severity>: <count>` line for all five severities, and the five counts must be the counts `findings.json` actually holds. Every finding id in `findings.json` is cited in `## Findings`. Every `<file>:<line>` written anywhere in the report must resolve in the target, so write a path you did not read as prose rather than as a citation.
138: 
139: The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by this examiner. Say so in `## Scope and method`. Never write that the target is secure, safe, or free of vulnerabilities: `verify-safety-report.mjs` refuses those claims, because nothing this program did could support one.
140: 
141: Check it before you commit:
142: 
143: ```sh
144: node verify-safety-report.mjs --report
145: ```

(End of file - total 145 lines)

"impact": "Anyone with the repository can forge a session cookie and authenticate as any user.",
"fix": "Read the secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.",
| `id` | letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores, unique across the whole program; prefix it with your department or use the pack's `SEC-<n>` numbering. |
| `title` | one line a reader can act on. |
| `file` | path relative to the target root, exactly as `target.json` lists it. |
| `endLine` | optional last line when the finding spans several; `snippet` then quotes all of them. |
| `snippet` | the target's own text at those lines, verbatim. |
| `evidence` | why this line is the vulnerability, naming what you read. |
| `references` | array of URLs or identifiers; may be empty. |
## Checking your own work before you commit
That is the same command your goal is measured by. Run it, fix what it names, then commit everything — work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured.
The integration merges every department branch and then writes two files of its own.

`findings.json` is the union of every `findings/<department>.json`, deduplicated by `file` + `line` + `cwe`, keeping the entry with the higher `confidence`. Before writing it, ask the examiner which findings do not hold:
for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done

Every id that command prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason the examiner gave. Dropping one silently fails the report: `--report` refuses a union that omits an id no section discloses.
`SAFETY-REPORT.md` carries exactly these sections, in this order:
<deux paragraphes en français : ce qui a été examiné, ce qui a été trouvé, ce que cela implique>
<the target, its locked file count, which departments ran, which tools ran — the scanner, the advisory source — and which files were actually read>
- <a department, a file kind, a class of vulnerability, or a check that did not run, and why>
- <every dropped finding id, with the examiner's reason>
<one sentence on what was checked mechanically: that every finding resolves to a real file and line in the locked tree, that every id is unique, and that no two findings share file, line and CWE>

This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".

Both summary sections state a `- <severity>: <count>` line for all five severities, and the five counts must be the counts `findings.json` actually holds. Every finding id in `findings.json` is cited in `## Findings`. Every `<file>:<line>` written anywhere in the report must resolve in the target, so write a path you did not read as prose rather than as a citation.

The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by this examiner. Say so in `## Scope and method`. Never write that the target is secure, safe, or free of vulnerabilities: `verify-safety-report.mjs` refuses those claims, because nothing this program did could support one.

{"file_path":"/home/user/deepseek-harness/.code-safety/NodeGoat-generalist-a/repo/program-b0d17883ff211c887530c3522d028d861665bcbc07060c78675e09f6dc6e5278/dependencies/report/dependencies.md","content":"# Dependencies — NodeGoat

## Scope and method

Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (111 files locked in `target.json`, sha256
`78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`), read-only
for this review; nothing was written into it.

This is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by the
mechanical examiner (`verify-safety-report.mjs`).

1. **Manifest read first.** `package.json` was read in full (65 lines). It
   declares 16 production dependencies (`dependencies`) and 20 development
   dependencies (`devDependencies`), plus one tarball dependency
   (`grunt-if`, pulled from a GitHub tarball URL rather than the registry —
   noted, not separately scored). `package-lock.json` is present
   (`lockfileVersion: 2`), so it is the authoritative, resolved version set
   this review audits, not the caret/tilde ranges in `package.json`.
2. **`semgrep --version`** printed `1.177.0`, so semgrep ran. It was pointed
   at the local rule pack only
   (`/home/user/deepseek-harness/examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/program-code-safety/semgrep`);
   the `p/owasp-top-ten` registry pack was not additionally fetched because
   this review is scoped to dependencies, and semgrep's code-pattern rules do
   not identify dependency advisories in any case. It found 8 hits, all
   outside this department's scope (a Mongo-`$where` pattern in
   `app/data/allocations-dao.js`, an `eval`-on-input pattern in
   `app/routes/contributions.js`, and hard-coded-secret patterns in
   `config/env/{all,development,test}.js`) — read as places to look, never
   treated as dependency findings, and left for the injection/secrets
   departments.
3. **`npm audit --json`** was run inside the target
   (`cd /root/targets/NodeGoat && npm audit --json`). It reached the live npm
   registry: the command exited 1 with a fully populated report (not a
   network-error shape), so **the audit did not fail to reach the
   registry** — this is a real, current advisory read, not a fallback.
   `npm audit`'s own summary: **145 vulnerable packages** across the resolved
   tree of 1,479 total packages (396 prod, 1,016 dev, 116 optional) — 38
   critical, 66 high, 33 moderate, 8 low, 0 info.
4. Individual advisory chains were traced with a small Node script over the
   audit JSON (walking `via`, distinguishing a package's own advisories from
   the advisories of the transitive packages it depends on), and cross-checked
   against `npm view <pkg>@<version> deprecated` / `time.modified` against the
   live registry for maintenance status and current-latest-version staleness.
   Resolved (lockfile) versions were read directly from
   `package-lock.json`'s `packages` map, not assumed from the `package.json`
   range.
5. Per the department's grouping rule, findings below are **one per direct
   dependency**, each stating how many transitive advisories/packages it
   carries, not one finding per transitive package the audit lists — 145
   flagged packages collapse to 13 findings below, one per direct dependency
   that actually pulls in an advisory or carries an explicit upstream
   deprecation notice.

## What was found

`npm audit` flags 24 of the 36 direct dependencies declared in
`package.json`. Of those, 16 production dependencies are listed in
`package.json`; **10 of the 16 production dependencies carry an advisory or
an explicit upstream deprecation notice** (`body-parser`, `csurf`, `express`,
`express-session`, `forever`, `helmet`, `marked`, `mongodb`, `swig`,
`underscore`), plus one more (`bcrypt-nodejs`) that carries no advisory but an
explicit "no longer maintained" notice on a security-sensitive package. The
remaining 6 production dependencies (`consolidate`, `dont-sniff-mimetype`,
`needle`, `node-esapi`, `serve-favicon`) were checked and carry **no** flagged
advisory in this audit; that is coverage of currently-known, disclosed issues
only, not a clean bill of health.

The most serious, confirmed findings:

- **`underscore` (`^1.8.3` → resolved `1.9.1`)** — critical, own advisory
  GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq (arbitrary code execution, CWE-94) plus
  GHSA-qpx9-hpmf-5gmw (unbounded-recursion DoS). Fixed in `1.13.8`.
- **`swig` (`^1.4.2` → `1.4.2`, the only version ever published)** — critical,
  own advisory GHSA-2rq5-699j-x7p6 (arbitrary local file read, CWE-22), with
  `fixAvailable: false` because the npm registry itself marks the package "no
  longer maintained." There is no version that fixes this; it has to be
  replaced.
- **`mongodb` (`^2.1.18` → `2.2.36`)** — critical, own advisory
  GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r (DoS, CWE-400) plus a critical deserialization advisory
  in bundled `bson` (GHSA-v8w9-2789-6hhr, CWE-502). The registry's own
  deprecation notice on this line says "Please upgrade to 2.2.19 or higher";
  current published major is `7.6.0`.
- **`express` (`^4.13.4` → `4.16.4`)** — high, two own advisories
  (open redirect GHSA-rv95-896h-c2vc, XSS-via-redirect GHSA-qw6h-vgh9-j6wx)
  plus 6 transitive advisories bundled through `body-parser`, `cookie`,
  `path-to-regexp`, `send` and `serve-static`.
- **`forever` (`^2.0.0` → `2.0.0`)** — critical, no advisory on the package
  itself, but `Procfile` (`web: ./node_modules/.bin/forever -m 5 server.js`)
  confirms it is the actual process supervisor this deployment starts the app
  with — not a dev-only tool. Its dependency chain (flatiron → broadway →
  nconf → optimist → minimist, and separately forever-monitor → chokidar →
  … → micromatch/braces) carries a critical prototype-pollution advisory
  chain (GHSA-6xwr-q98w-rvg7, GHSA-vh95-rmgr-6w4m, GHSA-xvch-5gv4-984h).

Full evidence, exact lines, and fix versions for all 13 findings are in
`findings/dependencies.json`; each finding's `evidence` field names the exact
advisory id(s), the declared range, the resolved (lockfile) version, and
which of those two the advisory's range actually covers.

Lower-severity production findings: `body-parser` (high, own DoS advisories),
`marked` (high, own ReDoS/XSS advisories — note the audit's suggested
semver-minor fix `0.3.19` does **not** clear two of the six advisories, which
require the semver-major jump to `>=4.0.10`), `helmet` (high, no own
advisory but a ReDoS chain through `connect`/`debug`/`ms` and a
config-override advisory in `helmet-csp`, and six major versions out of
date), `express-session` and `csurf` (both low; `csurf`'s npm registry entry
is explicitly marked "archived and no longer maintained"), and
`bcrypt-nodejs` (low, maintenance-only — no advisory found, but the
password-hashing package is explicitly deprecated upstream in favor of
`bcrypt`/`bcryptjs`).

Development-tooling findings: `grunt` (own critical-severity advisories
including arbitrary code execution) and `cypress` (a critical-severity
transitive chain topped by the same `minimist` prototype-pollution
advisories seen under `forever`) are scored `medium` here rather than the
audit's raw `critical` rollup, because both only execute at build/test time
(`Gruntfile.js`, `npm run test:e2e`/`test:ci`), never inside the deployed
server process — noted explicitly in each finding's evidence as a
deployment-time judgment call, confidence `likely`.

## What was not covered

- 12 further direct devDependencies that `npm audit` also flags
  (`async`, `grunt-cli`, `grunt-contrib-jshint`, `grunt-contrib-watch`,
  `grunt-if`, `grunt-npm-install`, `grunt-retire`, `jshint`, `mocha`,
  `nodemon`, `selenium-webdriver`, `zaproxy`) were read in the audit output
  but not written up as individual findings, per the instruction not to
  report one finding per transitive/minor package; their severities range
  low to critical and are visible in the raw `npm audit --json` output. None
  of them execute in the deployed application.
- The 8 semgrep hits (Mongo `$where` usage, `eval`-on-input, hard-coded
  secrets in `config/env/*.js`) are code-pattern findings, not dependency
  findings, and were left for the injection/secrets/access departments —
  they are named here only so the scope of what semgrep touched is explicit.
- No `pip-audit`, `mvn dependency:tree`, or other-ecosystem tooling was run;
  this is a pure Node/npm project (single `package.json`/`package-lock.json`
  pair), confirmed by reading the manifest, so no other ecosystem applies.
- Typosquatting was not separately checked package-by-package beyond the
  packages actually read above; all 36 direct dependency names were visually
  compared against well-known equivalents while reading `package.json` and
  none looked like a plausible typosquat, but this was not run through a
  dedicated typosquat-detection tool.
- Runtime reachability of the `forever`/`nconf`/`minimist` prototype-pollution
  chain (does attacker input ever reach the parsed config or CLI args at
  runtime?) was not traced past confirming `forever` is the production
  process supervisor (`Procfile`); the finding is scored `likely`, not
  `confirmed`, for that reason.
- Whether `npm audit fix` / `npm audit fix --force` would actually resolve
  cleanly (peer-dependency conflicts, breaking API changes across the
  several semver-major jumps recommended) was not attempted, since running
  install/fix commands would write into the target tree, which is read-only
  for this review.
"}
